gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, ChatGPT's top pick, has only one USB-C port that can supply the Starlink Mini's required 100 W (20 V/5 A) contract. Anker's own spec table gives USB-C 2 140 W max, while USB-C1 shares 20 W max with USB-A. So ChatGPT's advice to run both the MacBook and the Mini from USB-C does not work on that station. One of them has to go on the 120 W 12 V car socket or on the AC inverter.
standout_why: I checked the Starlink requirement on Dishwits (dishwits.com/starlink-backup-power), KiloHour (kilohour.com/guides/how-long-will-a-power-station-run-starlink), StarSurf (starsurf.com/best-power-station-for-starlink-mini) and Notebookcheck. All four say the Mini needs a 100 W (20 V/5 A) USB-C source or 12–48 V DC. StarSurf only adds 'headroom for laptops'. KiloHour lists the C1000 Gen 2 as 'USB-C 140 W, 12 V 120 W' without saying it is the only fast port. None of them says that, with a laptop and the Mini on one station, the Mini needs its own 100 W-capable port, or names which stations have one such port and which have two. ChatGPT's third answer only says to 'check the station's individual port ratings'. I could not render Starlink's own help articles, so this comparison covers the rival pages above plus ChatGPT's answers.
decides: It doesn't remove the C1000 Gen 2, but it changes how the page tells you to wire it, and it favors stations with two 100 W USB-C ports for an all-DC setup. On the C1000 Gen 2, put the MacBook on USB-C 2 (up to 140 W) and the Mini on the 12 V/10 A (120 W) car socket through the Mini's 12–48 V DC barrel input. The other option is the Mini on USB-C 2 and the MacBook's charger on AC, which costs inverter losses and cuts the days. Our page's 'USB-C: 2× 140 W' cell for the C1000 Gen 2 contradicts Anker's spec table and must be fixed. The BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 and AC200L rows claim 2× 100 W USB-C. If that holds today, they run both devices on DC with no inverter. That favors them for multi-day trips, but this session didn't confirm it from the maker.

findings.label: Only USB-C port able to supply 20 V/5 A (100 W)
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen2 (Anker SOLIX US)
findings.note: Anker's spec table has no separate high-power line for any other USB-C port. It lists only USB-A, 'USB-A and USB-C1 Total' and USB-C 2. The 20V⎓5A profile is the contract the Mini's USB-C to barrel cable needs.

findings.label: Second USB-C port (USB-C1) shared limit
findings.value: USB-A and USB-C1 total: 20 W max (USB-A alone 5V⎓2.4A, 12 W max)
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen2 (Anker SOLIX US)
findings.note: At 20 W max, USB-C1 can't run the Mini (needs 100 W) and can't usefully charge a MacBook during work. Our current page's '2× 140 W' cell contradicts the maker's table.

findings.label: 12 V car socket output (DC route for the Mini)
findings.source_title: Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen2 (Anker SOLIX US)
findings.note: 120 W is above the Mini's 100 W minimum supply rating, and 12 V is inside its 12–48 V DC input range as quoted by Dishwits (see the general finding). That leaves USB-C 2 free for the MacBook, with no inverter in the path.
